title: The morning Shema
hookLine: the Shema in the morning, even just the first line
tomorrow: one blessing before a meal. why does the Torah ask for one after?

lines: WHAT SHOULD A DAY LISTEN FOR?
cards: Earbuds in before breakfast: a podcast, a playlist, a voice telling you what to think about the day.
The morning starts by listening to something, and usually to several things at once: a news alert, the group chat, a song stuck in your head from last night.

One question for today: what should a day start by listening for? Jews have answered with the same line, morning and night, for a very long time. And the first thing it asks you to do isn't to believe, or to act.

teach.b: The line is from Deuteronomy: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew, the first word is Shema, hear, and the whole passage takes its name from it.

teach.h: WHEN THOU LIEST DOWN, AND RISEST UP.
teach.b: A few verses later comes the instruction to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So the Shema bookends the day, morning and night.

The Talmud tells that Rabbi Judah the Prince covered his eyes when he said the first line, and Jews still do it: eyes covered, the world shut out for one sentence, nothing to look at, only something to hear.
Even the first line alone, said in the morning with meaning, is a beginning. Now a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE.
teach.b: Muslims recite a short chapter of the Qur'an, Surah al-Ikhlas, which in Pickthall's translation opens: "Say: He is Allah, the One!" Shared ground: God's oneness, said aloud, in words people carry by heart.
And an honest difference, right in the first word. The Shema opens with hear, a call to a people, Israel, to listen together.
Al-Ikhlas opens with say, a declaration the Qur'an gives the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to proclaim. One begins by listening; the other by speaking.
Each tradition reads its own line in its own way, and neither needs the other's to be the same. For a Jewish morning, the order matters: before you say anything, hear.

how: Jews say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime, covering the eyes for the first line; the first line is also among the first prayers Jewish children learn.

o: a sunrise song sung by a synagogue choir
the line 'hear, O Israel' said as the day begins
a call to pray that's announced from a tower

games.q: hear and say — tap the pairs.
p: when thou liest down and risest up
covered his eyes for the first line

s: the Shema begins with a command to believe
it begins with hear. listening comes first.
Deuteronomy asks for these words when you lie down and when you rise up
that's why the Shema bookends the day, morning and night.
the Shema and Surah al-Ikhlas say exactly the same thing in the same way
both speak of God's oneness; the Shema opens with hear, to a people, and al-Ikhlas with say, a declaration.

games.q: your phone's first notification hits before you're out of bed, and you're tempted to answer. by the morning Shema, what comes first?
o: one line of listening before you answer anyone.
answer quickly, then you'll be calm enough to pray.
skip the line today; it only works if the morning is quiet.
games.why: the Shema opens with hear and is said as you rise up. before the day's voices, one sentence of listening.

practice: Cover your eyes with one hand, the way people do for the Shema's first line. If you say it, say it once, slowly, out loud or in a whisper: Shema Yisrael.
If not, simply listen, eyes covered, to whatever you can hear around you for the rest of the sit. Let one sound at a time have your whole attention.

wordCard.voice: The morning Shema: hear, O Israel, said as the day begins, often with the eyes covered. Listening first.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear. The first word of Deuteronomy 6:4 and the name of the whole passage.

carryVoice: Your line: hear, every morning. Listen before you say a word. Day one thousand six hundred fifty-one.
